title: Geometric prime quotients above a finite residue field
statement: Let $k$ be a field, $\Omega/k$ an algebraically closed field extension [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and $T$ a commutative $k$-algebra. Let $\mathfrak p\subset T$ be maximal and suppose that $F=T/\mathfrak p$ is finite-dimensional over $k$ [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Put $S=T\otimes_k\Omega$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For every prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ with inverse image $\mathfrak p$ under $t\mapsto t\otimes1$, the canonical map $F\otimes_k\Omega\to S/\mathfrak q$, $\bar t\otimes\lambda\mapsto(t\otimes\lambda)\bmod\mathfrak q$, is a well-defined surjective $\Omega$-algebra homomorphism and $S/\mathfrak q$ is finite-dimensional over $\Omega$. Moreover $\mathfrak q$ is maximal and both structural maps $\Omega\to S/\mathfrak q$ and $\Omega\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ are isomorphisms of $\Omega$-algebras, where $\kappa(\mathfrak q)=S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak qS_{\mathfrak q}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime].

source.place: Tag 00FV (theorem-nullstellensatz), finite residue field and algebraically closed case; explicit tensor-quotient version of the finite-dimensional argument in the geometric field-stalk descent, original proof steps 3-4.

proof.text: Write $B=S/\mathfrak q$ and $\pi:S\to B$ for the quotient map. Since the inverse image of $\mathfrak q$ is $\mathfrak p$, replacing $t$ by $t+u$ with $u\in\mathfrak p$ changes $\pi(t\otimes\lambda)$ by $\pi((u\otimes1)(1\otimes\lambda))=0$. Thus $\beta:F\times\Omega\to B$, $(\bar t,\lambda)\mapsto\pi(t\otimes\lambda)$, is well-defined and $k$-bilinear. The tensor universal property gives $h:F\otimes_k\Omega\to B$ with this formula. Using $(x\otimes a)(y\otimes b)=xy\otimes ab$ in these algebra tensor products, $h$ preserves products on pure tensors, hence on their finite sums, and sends $1\otimes1$ to $1$. Moreover $h(1\otimes\lambda)=\pi(1\otimes\lambda)$ and $h(\bar t\otimes\lambda\mu)=\pi(1\otimes\mu)h(\bar t\otimes\lambda)$; hence it is an $\Omega$-algebra homomorphism. Every element of $B$ lifts to a finite sum $\sum_i t_i\otimes\lambda_i$ in $S$, and is the image of $\sum_i\bar t_i\otimes\lambda_i$. Therefore $h$ is surjective.

source.place: Tag 00CX (lemma-tensor-product), universal property and pure-tensor generators; Section 00AR (section-rings-basic), quotient rings.

proof.text: Choose a finite $k$-spanning family $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $F$, using its assumed finite dimension. If $x=\sum_j c_je_j$ with $c_j\in k$, the tensor relations give $x\otimes\lambda=\sum_j e_j\otimes(c_j\lambda)$. Since pure tensors generate, the elements $e_j\otimes1$ span $F\otimes_k\Omega$ over $\Omega$. Surjectivity and $\Omega$-linearity of $h$ then show that $h(e_j\otimes1)$ span $B$ over $\Omega$. This proves the required finite dimensionality of $B$.

source.place: Tag 00CX (lemma-tensor-product), explicit bilinearity relations and generators; finite spanning-family argument.

proof.text: The ideal $\mathfrak q$ is prime, so $B$ is nonzero and has no zero divisors: $\pi(x)\pi(y)=0$ means $xy\in\mathfrak q$, hence $x\in\mathfrak q$ or $y\in\mathfrak q$. With the $\Omega$-algebra structure and finite dimension just established, apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dimensional-domain-is-field] to conclude that $B$ is a field. Consequently $\mathfrak q$ is maximal: any ideal strictly containing it gives a nonzero ideal of $B$, which contains a nonzero element and its inverse and therefore contains $1$.

Apply [lem-weil-pbc-alg-closed-finite-extension-trivial] to the field $B$, finite-dimensional over the algebraically closed field $\Omega$. Its conclusion is bijectivity of the actual structural map $i:\Omega\to B$, $\lambda\mapsto\pi(1\otimes\lambda)$. The inverse of a bijective algebra homomorphism is an algebra homomorphism, so this gives the asserted $\Omega$-algebra isomorphism, with its specified structural map.

source.place: Tag 09GR (lemma-algebraically-closed), equivalence with triviality of algebraic field extensions.
